hook: Kick a soccer ball and it flies off; let go of a phone and it drops; lean on a wall and the wall holds you up. Each of these is an interaction between two objects. Learning to see every interaction acting on one object, and to draw them as a free-body diagram, is the single most tested skill in this course.

prereq.why: A force has a size and a direction, so it is a vector. Mass, distance and time are sizes only.

prereq.q: On a line, a 30 m/s velocity to the right and a 10 m/s velocity to the left are written as
options: 30 m/s and 10 m/s, with no sign
prereq.why: Pick right as positive; then left is negative.

prereq.q: The center of mass of a system is
options: its geometric middle in every case
the point where it touches the ground
prereq.why: x_cm = Σm·x ÷ Σm weights each position by its mass.

figure.caption: Each force on the crate, drawn from a dot and labeled with its type and agent. Velocity stays in the scene.

chain.cause: Two objects interact (they touch, or one is Earth)
chain.effect: each exerts a force on the other: a push or pull with a size and a direction

chain.cause: You choose one object and list everything that touches it, plus Earth
chain.effect: you have every force on it, each with an agent

chain.cause: You draw each force as an arrow starting on a dot at the center of mass
chain.effect: you get a free-body diagram: whole forces, labeled with type and agent, lengths in proportion

chain.cause: You add the forces as vectors, with signs on each axis
chain.effect: you get the net force, which is a result of the diagram, not one of its arrows

ideas: A force is a push or pull between two objects, measured in newtons (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²). It is a vector.
Contact forces (normal force, tension, friction) need touching. Weight, F_g = mg, is Earth's pull at a distance; near Earth g = 9.8 m/s² (10 m/s² is accepted).
A free-body diagram: a dot for the object, one arrow per force starting on the dot, labeled type and agent ("F_N, floor on box"), no components, no velocity, no net force arrow.
The net force is the vector sum of all the forces. Find it from the diagram; never draw it on the diagram.

misconception.wrong: A moving object has a "force of motion" pushing it along, and the free-body diagram should show it.
misconception.right: Every force needs an agent touching the object (or Earth). Once a thrown ball leaves the hand, only Earth (and air) act on it. Motion does not need a forward force.

summary: A force is an interaction between two objects. To draw a free-body diagram, list every object touching your object plus Earth, and draw each force as a whole arrow from a dot, labeled with type and agent; the net force is their vector sum and is never drawn as an extra arrow.
